background: In March 2021, the world's largest eyewear company Luxoticca suffered a data breach via one of their partners that exposed the personal information of more than 70M people . The data was subsequently sold via a popular hacking forum in late 2022 and included email and physical addresses, names, genders, dates of birth and phone numbers.
In a statement from Luxottica, they advised they were aware of the incident and are currently "considering other notification obligations".
how: The published account does not explain the exact way the data was obtained.
outcome: 77,093,812 accounts are listed in this breach. This is a count of accounts, not necessarily individual people.
The reported exposed data includes Dates of birth, Email addresses, Genders, Names, Phone numbers, Physical addresses.
editorial: Two details in this record deserve more attention than the headline number. The first is that it happened through a partner, which meant the 70 million people in the file had no relationship with the company whose name is on it, they bought glasses from a brand Luxottica owns, or had an eye test at an optician it supplies. The second is the interval. The intrusion dates to March 2021.

The data was sold on a hacking forum in late 2022. For roughly eighteen months the exposure existed and there was nothing for anyone in it to read, act on or be notified about. A company's statement that it is "considering other notification obligations" is the sound that gap makes. Nothing in the exposed fields can be changed.
Name, date of birth, address, phone number and gender are the permanent identifiers, and the practical consequence is a phone call, some years later, from somebody who already knows all five.

fields.name: Physical addresses
fields.why: Where someone actually lives. Combined with a name this moves the risk off the internet.

fields.name: Phone numbers
fields.why: Enables SIM-swap attacks against SMS two-factor codes, and puts the number on scam-call lists indefinitely.

fields.name: Dates of birth
fields.why: One of the three things call centres ask to verify identity, and it never changes.

fields.name: Names
fields.why: Turns an anonymous address into an identified person, which is what makes targeted phishing possible.

fields.name: Email addresses
fields.why: The address becomes a confirmed, active target, expect more phishing, better aimed.

fields.name: Genders
fields.why: Small on its own; useful to anyone assembling a fuller profile.

actions: Move two-factor authentication off SMS and onto an authenticator app, which a SIM swap cannot intercept.
Be sceptical of post and callers who already know your address, knowing it is no longer evidence of anything.
Expect better-aimed phishing. A message that already knows your name and where you have an account is the whole point of a breach like this.
breach.scale_line: That is roughly everyone in the United Kingdom.
